topics.title: How do you build reusable components?
topics.html:
• Single responsibility — one component, one job.
  • Inversion of control via props, render props, or children.
  • Composition over configuration — Compound components beat 20 boolean props.
  • forwardRef on root + spread ...rest. In React 19 ref is just a prop.
const Button = forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(
  ({ children, variant = "primary", size = "md", ...rest }, ref) => (
    <button ref={ref} className={cn(styles.btn, styles[variant], styles[size])} {...rest}>
      {children}
    </button>
  )
);
// React 19 — ref is a plain prop, forwardRef not needed
function Button({ ref, children, ...rest }: ButtonProps & { ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement> }) {
  return <button ref={ref} {...rest}>{children}</button>;
}
💬 Say it like this

Think of a component like a LEGO brick — it does one thing. You pass data in through props, and it accepts children for flexibility. If you find yourself adding a fifth boolean prop to make it behave differently, that's your signal to break it into separate components or use the compound pattern.

I also always spread ...rest onto the root element so callers can pass any native HTML attribute without me forwarding them one by one.

How do you keep a component API from sprawling?
Compound pattern (Menu + Menu.Item), slot-based children. Fifth boolean prop = rethink the design.
What is a polymorphic component?
Renders as different HTML tags via an as prop — Box, Text, Button. Typed with generic ElementType.

topics.title: useMemo and useCallback — when to use and when NOT to.
topics.html:
• useMemo memoizes a value; useCallback memoizes a function (just useMemo(() => fn, deps)).
  • Use useMemo only for expensive computations. Use useCallback only when passed to React.memo child or used as useEffect dep.
  • Don't use by default — memoization costs memory. Profile first with React DevTools Profiler.
  • React 19 + Compiler: most manual memoizations become unnecessary.
💬 Say it like this

useMemo caches a calculated value, useCallback caches a function reference. Both re-run only when dependencies change. But the key thing is: don't reach for them by default. React renders are actually pretty fast. The problem is only when you pass unstable references to React.memo children or use them in useEffect deps.

I always profile first in DevTools — if I can't see the slow render in the flame graph, adding memo is just noise that makes the code harder to read.

What is referential equality and why does it matter for React.memo?
Objects/functions get new references on every render. memo compares with ===, so unstabilised props always look "changed" and memo does nothing.
What is a stale closure?
Function captures values at creation time. Incomplete dep array → reads stale state. Fix: useRef for values needed without re-subscribing, or fix deps.

topics.title: Compound Components — what and why?
topics.html:
Parent manages state via Context; child components are UI pieces reading from that context. No prop drilling. Used for: Tabs, Select, Accordion, Modal, Stepper.

const TabsCtx = createContext<TabsCtxType | null>(null);
function Tabs({ children, defaultTab }: TabsProps) {
  const [active, setActive] = useState(defaultTab);
  return (
    <TabsCtx.Provider value={{ active, setActive }}>
      <div role="tablist">{children}</div>
    </TabsCtx.Provider>
  );
}
Tabs.Tab = function Tab({ id, children }: TabProps) {
  const ctx = useContext(TabsCtx);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error("Tab must be used inside <Tabs>");
  return <button role="tab" aria-selected={ctx.active === id} onClick={() => ctx.setActive(id)}>{children}</button>;
};
💬 Say it like this

The parent holds state and children are visual pieces that connect to it through Context — not props. Classic example: <Tabs>. You write <Tabs.Tab> without passing active tab ID down manually. No prop drilling, and the user of the component decides how to arrange the children.

In React 19, anything new about Context?
You can render Context directly without .Provider. Less ceremony, same semantics.

topics.title: What is React Fiber and how does it work?
topics.html:
• Fiber is the unit of work: React 16+ redesigned its engine. Instead of synchronously traversing the entire component tree in one shot, React breaks the work into small units called "fibers" and schedules them across multiple frames.
  • Problem it solves: In React 15 (Stack Reconciler), if reconciliation took 50ms and you had 16.67ms per frame at 60fps, the main thread would block, causing jank (dropped frames, unresponsive UI). Fiber lets React interrupt work, yield to the browser, then resume.
  • Each fiber represents one component or DOM node: It's a JavaScript object with references to:
    • type: component function or tag name
    • props: props passed to this component
    • parent, child, sibling: tree structure (linked list)
    • state, hooks: component state
    • alternate: pointer to the "old" fiber from the previous render (for diffing)
    • effectTag: what to do with this fiber (PLACEMENT, UPDATE, DELETION)
  • Two-phase approach:
    • Render phase (can be interrupted, non-blocking): Reconciliation happens here. React builds a new fiber tree by running component functions, comparing with the old tree (via alternate), marking which fibers need changes. Can be paused/resumed.
    • Commit phase (synchronous, can't interrupt): React applies all marked changes to the actual DOM in one batch. Runs lifecycle methods (componentDidMount, effects). This is fast and must be atomic.
  • Scheduler: React uses a priority queue. Updates have priority:
    • Immediate (synchronous): flushSync(), state setters during event handlers
    • High: user input (click, input)
    • Normal: data fetching, timers
    • Low: background work
    High-priority work can interrupt low-priority work mid-render.
  • Work loop: React has a scheduler that on each frame:
    • Checks if there's work queued
    • Performs one fiber's work (run component, compare with alternate, create children)
    • Checks if frame budget (~5ms) is exhausted
    • If yes, yield to browser (let events, scrolls, paints happen)
    • Browser schedules MessageChannel or requestIdleCallback to continue
    • Resume when browser has free time
  • Why "alternate"?: During render phase, React doesn't mutate the old tree. It marks a new tree (Work in Progress, WIP). Once render completes, WIP tree becomes the "current" tree via finishWork(). This allows render phase to be retried without losing the current, committed tree.
// Conceptual fiber structure
const fiber = {
  type: MyComponent,
  props: { name: "Pavel" },
  state: { count: 0 },
  parent: parentFiber,
  child: childFiber,
  sibling: siblingFiber,
  alternate: oldFiber, // previous render's fiber
  effectTag: "UPDATE",
  hooks: [/* useState, useEffect, etc */],
  memoizedState: null, // for hooks
  memoizedProps: { name: "Pavel" }
};

// Work loop pseudocode
while (workQueue.length > 0 && frameHasTimeLeft()) {
  const fiber = workQueue.shift();
  performUnitOfWork(fiber); // run component, reconcile, mark changes
}
if (workQueue.length === 0) {
  commitRoot(); // apply all DOM changes atomically
} else {
  scheduleCallback(continueWorkLoop); // resume next frame
}
💬 Say it like this

Fiber is how React breaks rendering work into tiny chunks. Before Fiber (React 15), once React started reconciling, it couldn't stop until the entire tree was processed. If that took 100ms, the UI would freeze for 100ms. Fiber lets React do a little work, pause, check if the browser needs to handle user input or paint, then resume. Each component/element is a fiber — a data structure with its type, props, state, and a pointer to its previous version (the alternate). React maintains two fiber trees: the current one on screen, and a new one being built. During the render phase, React builds the new tree and marks which fibers changed. The commit phase happens all at once — React applies all the marked changes to the actual DOM. The key insight: render phase is interruptible, commit phase is not. That's why Concurrent React features like useTransition and Suspense work — they let high-priority updates interrupt low-priority ones during the render phase.

What's the difference between Work in Progress and current tree?
Current tree is the one rendered on screen. WIP tree is being built during render phase. They share fibers via the alternate pointer. Once render completes, WIP becomes current via finishWork(). This prevents mutations to the on-screen tree during rendering.
Why can render phase be interrupted but commit can't?
Render phase just builds metadata — it doesn't touch the real DOM. Interrupting it is safe; you can throw it away and restart. Commit phase mutates the DOM and runs lifecycle code. If you interrupted mid-commit, the DOM would be in an inconsistent state and effects would run partially. Commit must be atomic.
What happens if high-priority work arrives during low-priority render?
React abandons the current WIP tree and starts a new one for the high-priority update. The old WIP is thrown away. This is called "bailing out" or "render starvation prevention". That's how useTransition lets you interrupt long renders — the transition is low-priority, and user clicks are high-priority.
Does Fiber slow down React?
No. Fiber has small overhead (tracking pointers, checking frame budget), but the benefit is huge: you get non-blocking rendering. Concurrent features are opt-in, so basic React apps see no change. And because interruption is possible, you can use larger components without freezing the UI.

topics.title: What is reconciliation?
topics.html:
• Reconciliation is how React figures out what changed between renders.
  • When state updates, React re-runs the component and produces a new element tree.
  • It then diffs the new tree against the previous one to find the minimum number of DOM changes needed.
  • Only those specific DOM nodes are updated — not the whole page.
  • Two heuristics make this O(n): elements of different type produce a different tree; keys tell React which list items are the same across renders.
💬 Say it like this

When you call setState, React runs your component function again and gets a new description of the UI. Then it compares that new description with the old one — that comparison is reconciliation. If the component type is the same, it updates in place; if it changes, it destroys and rebuilds.

The key insight is that reconciliation produces a "list of changes" — then React applies only those changes to the real DOM. This is why React stays fast even when components re-render often. Keys in lists help React identify which item is which across renders, so it doesn't accidentally destroy and recreate the wrong elements.

topics.title: What does re-rendering mean in React?
topics.html:
• Re-rendering means React calls your component function again.
  • Triggered by: setState, parent re-rendering, context value changing.
  • Re-rendering does NOT automatically mean DOM updates — reconciliation decides what actually changes in the DOM.
  • A component re-render with identical output = zero DOM mutations.
💬 Say it like this

Re-rendering just means React calls your function again. It's actually cheap — the function runs, React gets a new description, reconciliation compares it, and if nothing changed in the output, zero DOM work happens.

The expensive part is when DOM operations actually fire, or when a component's render function does heavy computation — like filtering 10,000 items on every keystroke. That's where useMemo helps. But re-rendering itself is normal. You don't want to eliminate re-renders; you want to eliminate expensive work inside them.

topics.title: Why does React recommend against mutating state?
topics.html:
• React uses === to check if state changed. Mutate an object → same reference → React sees no change → no re-render.
  • Mutations make debugging harder — you lose the previous state so you can't compare "before" and "after".
  • Concurrent React can render multiple versions of the same state simultaneously — mutations corrupt this.
// BAD — React doesn't detect this change
const user = state.user;
user.name = "Pavel"; // mutation! same reference
setState(user); // React sees same object → no re-render

// GOOD — new reference, React detects change
setState({ ...state.user, name: "Pavel" });

// Immer handles deep updates cleanly
import { produce } from "immer";
setState(produce(draft => { draft.user.name = "Pavel"; }));
💬 Say it like this

React's change detection is based on reference equality — it uses ===. If you mutate an object in place, the reference stays the same, so React thinks nothing changed and won't re-render. You have to return a new object or array.

There's also a practical debugging reason: immutability lets you keep a history of state. Tools like Redux DevTools rely on this — if you mutate in place, you lose the ability to see what the state was before the change.

topics.title: Context API — Performance Patterns
topics.html:
Context re-renders every consumer on any value change. Strategy: split contexts by update frequency.

// BAD: one context for everything
const AppCtx = createContext({ user, theme, cart, notifications });

// GOOD: split by frequency
const UserCtx = createContext<User | null>(null);    // changes rarely
const CartCtx = createContext<CartState>(initialCart); // changes often

// Pattern: stable dispatch + separate state context
const CartDispatchCtx = createContext<Dispatch<Action>>(() => {});
// CartDispatchCtx value never changes → button components never re-render
💬 Say it like this

Context has one important limitation: any time the value changes, every component that reads it re-renders. So if you put everything in one context — user, theme, cart — a cart update re-renders your header too.

Fix: split contexts by how often they change. An even better pattern for write-heavy contexts: separate the dispatch function from the state. The dispatch function is stable (never changes), so components that only need to dispatch actions never re-render on state changes.

When is Context the wrong choice?
When the value changes frequently (text input, scroll position, websocket messages). Every consumer re-renders. Use Zustand or a selector library instead.

topics.title: Custom Hooks — Practical Gallery
topics.html:
Custom hooks extract and reuse stateful logic. The hook name must start with use.

// useDebounce — delay a value update
function useDebounce<T>(value: T, delay: number): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}
// usePrevious — track previous value
function usePrevious<T>(value: T): T | undefined {
  const ref = useRef<T>();
  useEffect(() => { ref.current = value; });
  return ref.current;
}
// useLocalStorage — synced with localStorage
function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key) ?? "null") ?? initial; }
    catch { return initial; }
  });
  const set = useCallback((v: T) => {
    setValue(v); localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(v));
  }, [key]);
  return [value, set] as const;
}
💬 Say it like this

A custom hook is just a function that calls other hooks. I use them to take stateful logic out of a component so I can reuse it and test it separately.

My rule is simple: if the same useState plus useEffect pair appears in two components, it becomes a hook. The name has to start with use so the linter can check the rules of hooks.

topics.title: Explain Concurrent React — useTransition, useDeferredValue, Suspense.
topics.html:
• Concurrent rendering: React can pause, interrupt, and resume renders.
  • Automatic batching in React 18: setState from setTimeout/Promises/native events all batch.
  • useTransition: mark an update as non-urgent. UI stays responsive, gives isPending flag.
  • useDeferredValue: defer a value from props/state when you can't reach the setter.
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const [list, setList] = useState(items);

const handleSearch = (val: string) => {
  setQuery(val); // urgent: input updates immediately
  startTransition(() => { // non-urgent: deferred
    setList(items.filter(i => i.name.includes(val)));
  });
};
💬 Say it like this

Before React 18, once a render started it had to finish. Now React can interrupt a low-priority render if something more urgent comes in — like a user typing. useTransition is how you tell React "this update is not urgent." You wrap the slow state update with startTransition, the input stays responsive, and you get an isPending flag to show a skeleton.

useDeferredValue does something similar but for values you receive — useful when you can't control where the setter is called, like a value coming from a library.

useTransition vs useDeferredValue?
useTransition wraps the setState call — you control what's deferred, get isPending. useDeferredValue defers a value you receive from outside (props, lib).
What is tearing in concurrent mode?
Different UI parts read different versions of external store during interrupted render. Fix: useSyncExternalStore (Redux Toolkit uses it internally).

topics.title: useEffect — antipatterns and useLayoutEffect.
topics.html:
• useEffect: async, after paint. For data fetching, subscriptions, side effects.
  • useLayoutEffect: sync, after DOM mutation but before paint. For DOM measurements, syncing animations.
// ANTIPATTERN: derived state in effect
useEffect(() => { setFullName(first + " " + last); }, [first, last]);
// FIX: compute during render
const fullName = first + " " + last;

// ANTIPATTERN: two chained effects
useEffect(() => { if (userId) fetchUser(userId).then(setUser); }, [userId]);
useEffect(() => { if (user) fetchPosts(user.id).then(setPosts); }, [user]);
// FIX: one effect, parallel fetches
useEffect(() => {
  if (!userId) return;
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  Promise.all([fetchUser(userId), fetchPosts(userId)])
    .then(([user, posts]) => { setUser(user); setPosts(posts); });
  return () => ctrl.abort();
}, [userId]);
💬 Say it like this

The most common mistake is putting derived data into an effect. If you can compute something from existing state or props during render, just do it there. No need for an effect, no extra render cycle.

useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before the browser paints. You need it when measuring DOM nodes and need to set something based on that measurement — otherwise you'd see a flash of wrong positioning.

Effect runs twice in dev — why?
React Strict Mode intentionally mounts/unmounts to surface missing cleanup. Production unaffected. Fix the cleanup, don't suppress.

topics.title: Error Boundaries
topics.html:
• Class components that catch render-time errors, show fallback UI. Via componentDidCatch + getDerivedStateFromError.
  • Don't catch: async errors, event handlers, SSR, the boundary itself.
  • Modern: react-error-boundary with resettable API and resetKeys.
import { ErrorBoundary } from "react-error-boundary";
<ErrorBoundary
  FallbackComponent={ErrorScreen}
  onReset={() => queryClient.resetQueries()}
  resetKeys={[userId]}
>
  <UserDashboard />
</ErrorBoundary>

BASIC Q — useRef vs forwardRef vs useImperativeHandle

  • useRef: mutable value surviving re-renders without causing them. DOM access, timer ids.
  • forwardRef (pre-19): lets parent attach ref to inner DOM node. React 19: ref is just a prop.
  • useImperativeHandle: customize what ref exposes — { focus(), reset() } instead of raw node.
function TextInput({ ref, ...rest }: Props & { ref?: Ref<InputHandle> }) {
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    focus: () => inputRef.current?.focus(),
    clear: () => { if (inputRef.current) inputRef.current.value = ""; },
  }), []);
  return <input ref={inputRef} {...rest} />;
}
💬 Say it like this

An error boundary catches an error during rendering and shows a fallback screen instead of a blank page. Only class components can do it, so in practice I use the react-error-boundary library.

It does not catch everything though. Errors in event handlers, in async code and on the server are not caught, so those still need normal try/catch. I usually put one boundary around the whole app and smaller ones around risky parts, like a widget or a chart.

topics.title: Rules of Hooks — not the rules, the reason.
topics.html:
• Hooks are stored on the fiber as an ordered linked list. React doesn't know a hook's name — it knows it's the first, second, third call of this render.
  • So a conditional hook shifts the list: on the next render, useState at position 2 reads the memory cell that belonged to useEffect. That's why the error is "rendered fewer hooks than expected", not "hook in an if".
  • Same reason hooks can't be called in loops with variable length, in event handlers, or in plain functions — no fiber, no list.
  • Custom hooks are just functions that call hooks; the rules apply transitively, which is why the linter tracks the use prefix.
  • Escape hatch when you truly need conditionality: always call the hook, and make the argument conditional (useQuery({ enabled: isReady })).
// BROKEN — the list shifts between renders
if (user) { const [name, setName] = useState(user.name); }

// FIX — hook always runs, condition moves inside
const [name, setName] = useState(user?.name ?? "");
const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["u", id], queryFn: fetchUser, enabled: !!id });
💬 Say it like this

React keeps hooks in an ordered list on the fiber and identifies each hook by its call order, not by its name. So if a hook is inside a condition, the order changes between renders and React gives your state to the wrong hook. That is the real reason for the rule. When I need something conditional, I still call the hook always and pass the condition as an option — like enabled in React Query.

Why does React 19's use() get to break this rule?
use() isn't stored in the hooks list the same way — it reads a promise or context during render and can suspend, so it's allowed in conditionals. It's the deliberate exception, not a loophole for other hooks.

topics.title: Two things interviewers use to check you really understand state: key and controlled inputs.
topics.html:
key as a reset mechanism — changing a key unmounts the old component and mounts a fresh one, dropping all its state. The idiomatic way to reset a form when the entity changes:

<ProfileForm key={userId} user={user} />   // switching user → clean form, no useEffect sync

// Anti-pattern this replaces:
useEffect(() => { setName(user.name); }, [user]);  // extra render, easy to get wrong

Controlled vs uncontrolled:

  • Controlled — value comes from state, every keystroke re-renders. Needed when you validate as you type, transform input, or drive other UI from it.
  • Uncontrolled — the DOM owns the value, read via ref or FormData on submit. Cheaper, and the default in React 19 form actions.
  • Switching a component from uncontrolled to controlled mid-life triggers React's warning — usually caused by an initial undefined value. Fix with ?? "".
  • Big forms: uncontrolled + react-hook-form beats controlled state for performance because typing doesn't re-render the whole form.
💬 Say it like this

Changing the key is the cleanest way to reset state. React treats it as a different component, so I do not need an effect that copies props into state. For forms I use uncontrolled inputs by default, unless I have to react to every keystroke, because a controlled input re-renders the form on every character and that is where big forms get slow.

topics.title: useSyncExternalStore — what is it for, and what is tearing?
topics.html:
• It's the official way to subscribe React to state that lives outside React: Zustand, Redux, a browser API, a WebSocket cache, matchMedia, navigator.onLine.
  • Tearing: with concurrent rendering, React can pause mid-render. If an external store changes during that pause, one part of the tree renders the old value and another the new one — the same state shown two ways in one frame.
  • useSyncExternalStore prevents it by forcing a synchronous, consistent read for that subscription (at the cost of opting that update out of concurrent tearing-avoidance).
  • Third argument getServerSnapshot exists for SSR — without it you get a hydration mismatch on anything browser-only.
const isOnline = useSyncExternalStore(
  (cb) => {                                   // subscribe → returns unsubscribe
    window.addEventListener("online", cb);
    window.addEventListener("offline", cb);
    return () => { window.removeEventListener("online", cb); window.removeEventListener("offline", cb); };
  },
  () => navigator.onLine,                     // client snapshot
  () => true                                  // server snapshot — avoids hydration mismatch
);
💬 Say it like this

It is the hook for connecting React to state that React does not own. The problem it solves is called tearing: with concurrent rendering React can pause in the middle of a render, and if the external store changes at that moment, different parts of the tree can show different values in the same frame. This hook guarantees one consistent snapshot. I rarely call it directly — Zustand and Redux use it inside — but I use it for browser state like online status or a media query.
